note:
Square face close-ups: women 35-40 from different ethnic backgrounds, each gently applying a small dab of cream to the cheek. 1:1, per Malcolm's brief.

ONE VARIABLE AT A TIME. Framing, lighting, ground and gesture are held IDENTICAL across all six slots, and only two things change: who she is, and the colour of the cream. That is deliberate - the point of the batch is to compare people and cream colours, and if the framing moved as well there would be no way to tell which difference was doing the work. It also means the six can be used together as a set on one page without looking like six unrelated shots.

ETHNICITY IS NAMED PER SLOT, NOT LEFT TO THE ENGINE. Asking six suppliers for 'different ethnic backgrounds' returns six versions of each engine's default face. Each slot therefore states one background, and the six between them cover East Asian, West African, South Asian, White European, Latin American and Middle Eastern. Age is stated as a range in every slot because a bare number tends to be read as 'young' by most engines.

CREAM COLOURS. Malcolm asked for white, light blue or dark blue. Each appears twice across the six, so every colour is seen on two different skin tones - which is the comparison that matters, since a pale cream reads very differently on deep skin than on fair skin.

WHAT 'A SWAB' HAD TO BE SPELLED OUT AS. Left as 'a swab of cream', engines produce either a cotton bud on a stick or a broad warpaint stripe. It is described here as a measured thing instead: a soft dab roughly the width of two fingertips, sitting on the cheekbone, with her own fingertips just touching its edge mid-motion. Same lesson as 'long pipette' and 'full forearm' - a measured description survives six engines where a named object does not.

SKIN. The whorl artefact that Malcolm caught on the PDRN hero - concentric fingerprint-like micro-lines on the cheek - is named in the negatives rather than wished away, and the positive side describes what real skin does. It matters more here than usual, because the cheek is the subject and it is the exact place that artefact appears.

NO PRODUCT IN FRAME, so there is no label to render and nothing for FLUX.2 to invent a brand on - it is included. Luma is left out: it has refused this subject family all session and costs three to four minutes per attempt to find that out again.

slots.title: East Asian, white cream
slots.prompt: Editorial beauty photograph, square format, close on the face of one East Asian woman between thirty five and forty years old, turned three quarters toward the camera so her near cheek faces the lens. The frame holds her from just above the eyebrows to the base of the neck, her cheek filling the middle of the picture. She is applying a small dab of WHITE cream to that cheekbone: a soft rounded dab roughly the width of two fingertips, sitting cleanly on the skin with a soft edge, and her own index and middle fingertips just touching its edge as if she has this moment begun to spread it. Her fingers are relaxed and her nails short, natural and unpainted. Her expression is calm and unposed, eyes open and looking softly past the camera, lips closed and relaxed. Almost no makeup. Real skin kept real: visible pores, natural fine lines at the eye and around the mouth, a few freckles or natural marks, fine down catching the light along the jaw, and uneven sheen so some areas read matte and others slightly shiny. The texture never resolves into swirls, whorls, concentric rings or any repeating pattern anywhere, least of all on the cheek. Hair simply worn and swept back from the face. Behind her a seamless deep graphite backdrop, colour #1A1A1A, falling to near-black at the edges. One large soft key from the upper left models the cheekbone and jaw, with one dim cool fill on the shadow side. 85mm at f4, very shallow depth of field with the cheek and the cream sharp, fine film grain, natural skin tones, quiet and expensive.
slots.negative_extra: blue cream, tinted cream, cream on the wrong cheek, hand covering the face, palm over the cheek, smiling broadly, open mouth
